title: Socialising and networking
subtitle: housewarming, black-tie, rub shoulders with
summary: Name every kind of party from a housewarming to a leaving do, and use the informal language of networking and social life.

lesson.heading: A hectic social life
lesson.text: In an email to a friend, Jess writes: 'Things have been really **hectic on the social front** here. It seems to be nothing but parties!' She then lists them all. Each one has its own name in English, and using the right one matters - you cannot invite someone to a hen night and mean a wedding reception.

examples.text: Frankie and Joe had their **housewarming** last week, now that they've decorated.
Josh went to his friend Mick's **stag party** last weekend - they went to Spain for it!
Next week, my old schoolmate Angela's having her **hen night**. It's **fancy dress** too.

lesson.heading: Nouns for social events
rows: a party to celebrate moving to a new house or flat
a party before a wedding for the future husband and his male friends
a night out before a wedding for the future wife and her female friends
the main group of close family and friends at a wedding
a formal party, for example after a wedding or to meet an important visitor
a formal event where men wear dinner jackets and bow ties, women evening dresses
a party to celebrate the publication of a new book or product
an evening out just for female friends
a party for somebody leaving a job or institution
lesson.note: Do is an informal noun for a party or celebration: our do, the office do.

left.label: Socialising
examples: I've got the usual **girls' night out** with Amy and Izzie every few weeks.
It was good at the club last night - Pete was there with his **crowd**.

right.label: Networking
right.text: Making contacts that are going to be useful to your business or career. Don't leave it to chance - plan your networking.
examples: **Exchange** business cards and **do lunch** with useful people.
Make sure you **rub shoulders with** the people who really matter.

lesson.heading: The language of networking
lesson.text: To **do lunch** is an informal way of saying have lunch together, usually to talk business. To **hobnob with** someone is to be friendly with an important or famous person - it often carries a note of disapproval. To **rub shoulders with** people is to mix socially with them (informal). Being **proactive** means taking action yourself rather than waiting for something to happen.

examples.text: Don't be afraid to **hobnob with** the boss. Go for it!
It irritates me the way he's always **hobnobbing with** the managers.
Try to be **proactive** in the workplace.

lesson.heading: Expressions for social activity
lesson.text: To **hang out with** or **knock around with** people is to spend social time with them (both informal). Someone's **crowd** is their group of friends. A **party animal** loves going to parties. A group that does not let others join them is **cliquey** - and the group itself is a **clique**, a disapproving word.

examples.text: I don't like the people Chris **hangs out with**.
I hate it at my new job - everyone's so **cliquey**.

lesson.heading: Guests and dates
lesson.text: If you **outstay your welcome**, you stay too long at someone's home. Two people in a romantic relationship are **an item** (informal). If someone **stands you up**, they simply don't arrive for a date you had arranged.

examples.text: I hope I'm not **outstaying my welcome**.
Lizzy and Rob are always together. Are they **an item**?
Joel isn't very happy because Molly **stood him up** last night.

lesson.text: Crowd is a singular noun with a plural feel: Laurie's crowd are really fun people.

exercises.prompt: What kind of party would you be invited to in each case?

pairs.left: Some friends have just moved into a new flat.
A friend has just had a book published.
The council is arranging for local dignitaries to meet a visitor.
Your friends love dressing up as characters from famous films.
A colleague is leaving the office for good.

exercises.prompt: A male friend is getting married and is having a party for his male friends before the wedding. What is it?
exercises.explanation: A stag party (or stag night) is for the future husband and his male friends; the hen party is the women's equivalent.

exercises.prompt: I'm going to a dinner at the Royal Plaza Hotel tonight. It's a ___ event, so I'll need my dinner jacket.
exercises.explanation: A black-tie event is a formal one where men wear dinner jackets and black bow ties.

exercises.prompt: We're going to have a ___ night out on Friday - no boyfriends, no husbands.
exercises.explanation: A girls' night out is an evening out just for female friends.

exercises.prompt: We must invite Jasmine to our do. She's a real party ___!
exercises.explanation: A party animal is someone who loves going to parties.

exercises.prompt: Don't always wait for people to do things for you. You should be more ___.
exercises.explanation: To be proactive is to take action yourself rather than wait for something to happen.

exercises.prompt: It's good to see you! We must ___ lunch sometime and discuss business.
exercises.explanation: To do lunch is an informal way of saying have lunch together, usually to talk business.

exercises.prompt: It's always good to see Theo, but somehow he always manages to ___ his welcome.
exercises.explanation: To outstay your welcome is to stay too long at someone else's home.

exercises.statement: He usually hangs over with his college friends at the weekend.
exercises.explanation: The phrasal verb is hang out: He usually hangs out with his college friends at the weekend.

exercises.statement: Nella and her friends are very clique. They don't mix with anyone else.
exercises.explanation: The adjective is cliquey: Nella and her friends are very cliquey.

exercises.statement: She said she wanted to go out with me, then she stood me up!
exercises.explanation: Correct - to stand someone up is to fail to arrive for a date you had arranged.

exercises.prompt: Rita and Nick have been together for months. Which sentence is right?
options: Rita and Nick are an item.
Rita and Nick are an article.
Rita and Nick are a crowd.
Rita and Nick are a clique.
exercises.explanation: Two people in a romantic relationship are an item (informal).

exercises.prompt: Don't forget your old friends when your film becomes a hit and you're ___ the rich and famous.
exercises.explanation: To rub shoulders with people is to mix socially with them; hobnobbing with is also possible here.

exercises.prompt: Is each expression about pure socialising, or about networking for business?
Put this piece of networking advice in order.
exercises.answer: Make sure you rub shoulders with the people who really matter
exercises.explanation: To rub shoulders with someone is to mix socially with them.
